title: Udyoga: the embassy, Krishna's counsel, Karna and Kunti
hook: Sanjaya arrives from the blind king with a message about peace, and Yudhishthira answers with a very small request
carry: five villages, and let this end
tomorrow: Udyoga: the embassy, Krishna's counsel, Karna and Kunti

segments.voice: Yesterday the Udyoga began at Krishna's bedside, and Arjuna chose Krishna over an army. Your line was whose face Krishna saw when he opened his eyes. Did you reach for a person or an advantage? Day eight hundred fourteen.

An envoy rides into the Pandava camp. It's Sanjaya, the trusted charioteer and counselor of the blind king Dhritarashtra. He greets everyone warmly, asks after their health, and then delivers his master's message. It isn't an offer. It isn't a threat. It's a plea: don't fight. Notice what's missing from the message. Dhritarashtra asks for peace, but he doesn't offer to give back what was taken. Today, an embassy that talks about peace and leaves out the price.
screen: `SANJAYA RIDES IN.` → `THE MESSAGE: DON'T FIGHT.` → `WHAT THE MESSAGE LEAVES OUT.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya speaks movingly, and the Pandavas don't brush it aside. A war between cousins, he says, means killing your own teachers, your own uncles, your own kin. What kind of victory is that? It would be better, he says, to live on alms than to win a kingdom that way. Yudhishthira listens, and his answer is not angry. I want peace too, he says. Who would choose war if peace were possible? But peace has to mean something. Give us back our own kingdom, Indraprastha, the city we built. Krishna speaks as well. Holding back from action, he says, is no answer by itself; a person must act, and act rightly. In Krishna's reply, Sanjaya's advice sounds holy but asks only one side to give anything up. And then, in this same exchange, Yudhishthira makes a request so small it's almost painful to hear. Not the whole kingdom. Not even the city. Give us five villages, he says, and let this end. Five villages, from men who once ruled. Sanjaya carries the message home. And in the next scenes of the book, we'll watch what the Kuru court does with it. Today, just stay with the shape of the exchange. One side talks about peace as the absence of fighting. The other talks about peace as fairness, and is willing to accept very little of it.
screen: `SANJAYA: DON'T FIGHT YOUR KIN` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: WE WANT PEACE TOO` · `KRISHNA: ACT, AND ACT RIGHTLY` · then, large: `EVEN FIVE VILLAGES`

segments.voice: Sit easily and let your breath come and go. Bring to mind a disagreement you're in, at home, at work, with a friend. Breathing in, ask: what would fairness look like here, for both of us? Breathing out, ask: what's the smallest thing that would let me make peace? Don't decide anything. Just let the two questions sit side by side. If you pray, you can bring that disagreement into your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Udyoga. The getting ready, where an envoy asks for peace, and Yudhishthira asks for five villages.
Your line: five villages, and let this end. Today, when someone asks you to keep the peace, ask what peace would be fair, and to whom. Day eight hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Yudhishthira's request for five villages is remembered in retellings of the Mahabharata as the very small price the Pandavas would accept for peace before the war.

pairs: better alms than a kingdom won by killing

myth: Sanjaya came offering to return the Pandavas' kingdom
he pleaded with them not to fight, without offering what was taken.
Yudhishthira said he wanted peace too
he answered calmly that no one would choose war if peace were possible.
Yudhishthira demanded the whole Kuru kingdom
he asked for Indraprastha, and said even five villages would do.

fork.setup: you're Yudhishthira. Sanjaya says war with your kin would be a terrible wrong, but offers nothing back. what do you answer?
options: agree, and stay in exile for good.
say you want peace too, and ask for your kingdom, or even five villages.
send Sanjaya away without an answer.
fork.reveal: he answers gently, asks for Indraprastha, and then for as little as five villages.

original.note: effort, getting ready; the book where both sides prepare, and envoys travel between them.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sanjaya was the peacemaker and the Pandavas wanted war.
what it means: Sanjaya asks only one side to give up its claim; Yudhishthira also wants peace, but a fair one.
what a scholar hears: 'five villages' shrinks the dispute to its plainest terms, and shows how little the Pandavas would accept.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Udyoga Parva (Sanjaya-yana), Sanjaya's embassy to the Pandavas, Yudhishthira's and Krishna's replies, and the request for five villages

notes: Audit: narrator's verdicts on Sanjaya ('much of what he says is true'; 'asks only one side to give everything up') reattributed to the story and to Krishna's reply, so the narrator doesn't judge the envoy.
All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli that Sanjaya's speech includes the idea that living on alms is better than winning by slaying kin.
Confirm Krishna's reply to Sanjaya on action versus inaction, summarized very briefly here.
The five villages: confirm where the request is made in Ganguli's text (to Sanjaya at the end of the Sanjaya-yana, naming four places and 'any other').
The hook's 'trusted charioteer and counselor' describes Sanjaya's role; check wording.
